To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the contact stress field in a half-space with alternating stiff and soft layers does not converge to the corresponding value in a fully homogenized half-space with increasing number of alternating layers, but to the contact stress field of a partially homogenized half-plane wherein the layered configuration is homogenized beneath a certain depth with surface layers retained.

the contact of layered half-planes with alternating stiff and soft layers leads to characteristic contact pressure profiles that can be used to identify the microstructural architecture of the layered half-plane.

the contact pressure and the subsurface stress field are not fully reproduced by a fully homogenized half-plane, but by a partially homogenized configuration wherein a finite number of surface layers are retained.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a methodology for the determination of surface and subsurface stresses in layered half-planes with large modulus contrast and the development of a new technique for the characterization of the microstructure and material properties of the subsurface layers.
the development of a new class of sensors that can be embedded in a structure to monitor its health, and also provide information about the structure's microstructural architecture.

the development and validation of efficient computational techniques to study the contact mechanics of layered structures with large moduli contrasts, and the application of these techniques to study the effect on the contact and subsurface stress field of microstructural refinement in the subsurface region of a multilayered half-plane.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the microstructure of a multilayer system can be characterized in a non-invasive manner by a combination of the contact pressure profile and the stress field in the subsurface region.

the stress fields in the layered configurations do not converge to those in the homogenized configurations, but that they converge to those in partially homogenized ones, wherein the top surface layers are retained.

a homogenized model with a depth of about three times the thickness of the surface layer would be sufficient to capture the stress fields in the layered configuration, and a homogenized depth of about 5 to 6 times the surface layer thickness would be sufficient to predict the surface contact pressure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the microstructural effects are significant for the surface contact pressure and stress field in multilayers with large moduli contrast.
the contact of layered materials is a promising technique to probe microstructural properties of the subsurface regions.

the microstructural effects in layered materials loaded in frictionless contact can be accurately captured by a partially homogenized model with the number of retained surface layer pairs depending on the punch length, the microstructural scale, and the depth of the alternating layer pairs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the contact response of a layered half-plane is not always accurately represented by the contact pressure and stress field in the fully homogenous configuration with the same macroscopic properties.
the contact problem of layered configurations is amenable to an accurate solution by a partial homogemization of the half-plane.
the contact pressure profile can be used as a signature to identify the microstructural architecture of the subsurface.
